scenarios.title: The Big-O of a mixed loop nest
scenarios.situation: A teammate analyzes a routine with an O(n) setup pass, an O(n^2) double loop, and an O(n log n) sort, then reports O(n^2 + n log n + n).
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct asymptotic bound, and why?
evidence:
setup:   O(n)
process:  O(n^2)   <- double loop
sort:     O(n log n)
claimed:  O(n^2 + n log n + n)
choices: O(n^2) — Big-O keeps only the dominant term as n grows; lower-order terms and constant factors are dropped
O(n^2 + n log n + n) — every phase contributes and must be listed
O(n^3) — the phases multiply because they run in sequence
O(n log n) — sorting dominates all polynomial loops
scenarios.why: Big-O describes growth rate as n→∞: the fastest-growing term eventually dwarfs the rest, so O(n^2 + n log n + n) simplifies to O(n^2). Sequential phases add (not multiply) — multiplication applies to nested loops. Constants are dropped because the notation compares shapes of growth, not exact step counts.
scenarios.hint: As n gets very large, which term outgrows the others — and what does Big-O keep?

scenarios.title: The append that is usually cheap
scenarios.situation: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. A reviewer claims append is O(n) because of the occasional resize.
scenarios.prompt: What is the amortized cost of append, and why?
evidence:
append x: if full, allocate 2x capacity and copy all n elements (O(n)), then insert (O(1))
resizes happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
choices: Amortized O(1) — the expensive resizes are geometrically spaced, so total copy work over n appends is O(n)
O(n) — the worst single append dominates the analysis
O(log n) — capacity doubles, so cost grows logarithmically
O(n^2) — each append may copy everything before it
scenarios.why: Resizes at sizes 1,2,4,...,n copy 1+2+4+...+n = 2n-1 total elements — a geometric series bounded by 2n. Spread over n appends, that is O(1) each on average. Amortized analysis averages the total cost of a sequence; it does not promise any single operation is cheap (a latency-sensitive system may still prefer pre-sized arrays).
scenarios.hint: Add up the copy work of every resize across n appends. What series is 1+2+4+...+n, and what does it sum to?

scenarios.title: The recursion that blew the stack, not the heap
scenarios.situation: A recursive binary-tree traversal uses O(1) extra heap but crashes with stack overflow on a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) tree.
scenarios.prompt: What is the space complexity, and why does the tree shape matter?
choices: O(h) call-stack space where h is tree height — O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate; the stack frames are the hidden space cost
O(1) — recursion uses no extra space beyond the input
O(n) always — every node gets a stack frame simultaneously
O(n^2) — each level re-scans the subtree
scenarios.why: Each recursive call holds a stack frame until its children return, so peak stack depth equals the longest root-to-leaf path: the tree height h. Balanced trees give O(log n); a degenerate chain gives O(n) — enough to overflow the call stack. Space analysis must count the call stack, not just allocated containers.
scenarios.hint: How many calls are on the stack at the deepest moment — and what determines that number?

scenarios.title: The sort that degrades on sorted input
scenarios.situation: Quicksort with a first-element pivot runs in O(n log n) on random data but O(n^2) on already-sorted input — exactly the input a pipeline produces.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the pivot choice cause quadratic behavior?
evidence:
pivot = first element
sorted input: every partition splits off 1 element and leaves n-1
T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n)  ->  O(n^2)
choices: A bad pivot makes partitions maximally unbalanced — random or median-of-three pivots make the worst case vanishingly unlikely
Sorted input is inherently quadratic for all comparison sorts
The partition loop is O(n^2) by itself — rewrite it
Quicksort is O(n^2) average-case — the random-data timing was luck
scenarios.why: Quicksort's O(n log n) average assumes roughly balanced partitions. A fixed first-element pivot on sorted input always picks the minimum, producing 1 vs n-1 splits: T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) = O(n^2). Randomizing the pivot (or median-of-three) makes adversarial input unlikely; the recurrence then averages to O(n log n). Worst-case O(n^2) remains theoretically possible but practically irrelevant.
scenarios.hint: What do the partition sizes look like when the pivot is always the smallest element?

scenarios.title: Why binary search is logarithmic
scenarios.situation: A junior engineer believes binary search is O(n) 'because it looks at elements one at a time like linear search'.
scenarios.prompt: How do you derive the O(log n) bound?
evidence:
each step discards half the range: n -> n/2 -> n/4 -> ... -> 1
halvings until 1: k where n / 2^k = 1  ->  k = log2(n)
choices: Each comparison halves the search space, so reaching one element takes log2(n) halvings — O(log n)
Binary search examines log n elements per step — O(n log n) total
The midpoint computation is O(1), so the whole search is O(1)
Halving is exponential decay, which is O(2^n) inverted — O(sqrt n)
scenarios.why: One comparison eliminates half the candidates. After k steps, n/2^k candidates remain; the search ends when one remains, so k = log2(n). The key insight: the work per step is constant and the problem size shrinks geometrically — that combination always yields logarithmic complexity.
scenarios.hint: If each step throws away half of what remains, how many steps until one element is left?

scenarios.title: The recurrence that keeps appearing
scenarios.situation: Merge sort's analysis gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). A teammate guesses O(n^2) 'because there are two recursive calls'.
scenarios.prompt: What does this recurrence solve to, and what is the intuition?
evidence:
T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)   (two halves + linear merge)
recursion tree: log n levels, O(n) work per level
choices: O(n log n) — the recursion tree has log n levels, each doing O(n) total merge work
O(n^2) — two subproblems means squaring
O(n) — the halves cancel out
O(2^n) — branching factor 2 gives exponential growth
scenarios.why: Draw the recursion tree: level 0 does O(n) merge work; level 1 has two nodes each merging n/2 (total O(n)); every level totals O(n). There are log2(n) levels (halving until size 1), so total work is O(n log n). This is the Master Theorem's case 2 (a=2, b=2, f(n)=Θ(n) = Θ(n^log_b a)).
scenarios.hint: At each level of the recursion tree, the subproblem sizes sum to n. How many levels are there?

scenarios.title: The pair sum in a sorted array
scenarios.situation: Given a sorted array, find two numbers summing to a target. The brute force is O(n^2); the interviewer wants O(n).
scenarios.prompt: How do the two pointers converge on the answer?
choices: Pointers start at both ends; if the sum is too small, advance lo (larger value needed); if too big, retreat hi — each step discards one element that cannot be part of any solution
Move both pointers inward every step — the middle pair is checked last
Start both at the middle and expand outward — symmetric coverage
Two pointers only work on unsorted arrays — sort a copy first
scenarios.why: Sortedness makes each comparison decisive: a[lo]+a[hi] < target means a[lo] is too small to pair with anything (even the largest a[hi]), so lo is eliminated; symmetrically for hi. Each step removes one candidate in O(1), giving O(n) total with O(1) space — no hash map needed.
scenarios.hint: When the sum is too small, which pointer can you prove is useless — and why does sortedness make that proof work?

scenarios.title: The longest substring without repeats
scenarios.situation: Find the longest substring with all unique characters. The O(n^2) check-every-substring approach times out.
scenarios.prompt: How does the sliding window achieve O(n)?
choices: Expand hi each step; when a duplicate appears, jump lo past its previous occurrence — each index enters and leaves the window once
Restart the window from scratch at each duplicate — simpler and still O(n)
Use two nested loops but break early on duplicates — average case O(n)
Sort the characters first, then scan — O(n log n) is close enough
scenarios.why: The window [lo, hi] always holds a valid (duplicate-free) substring. hi advances n times total; lo only moves forward (at most n times). Each character is processed a constant number of times — O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space for the last-seen map. The invariant 'window is always valid' is what makes one pass sufficient.
scenarios.hint: How many times can lo move forward across the whole run — and what does that imply about total work?

scenarios.title: The range sum asked a million times
scenarios.situation: An analytics service answers sum(l, r) queries over a static array. Each query scans the range: O(n) per query, too slow at scale.
scenarios.prompt: How do you answer each query in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing?
choices: Build a prefix-sum array P where P[i] is the sum of the first i elements; range sum(l,r) = P[r+1] - P[l]
Sort the array first — range sums are faster on sorted data
Cache query results in a dict — repeated queries hit the cache
Use a segment tree — O(log n) per query is the best possible
scenarios.why: P[r+1] - P[l] cancels the shared prefix: (a0+...+ar) - (a0+...+a{l-1}) = a{l}+...+ar. Preprocessing is O(n) time and space; every query is O(1). (Segment trees/Fenwick trees answer in O(log n) but support point updates — the right tool when the array changes; prefix sums win for static data.)
scenarios.hint: If you knew the sum of everything before l and everything through r, how would you isolate just [l, r]?

scenarios.title: The rotation without extra memory
scenarios.situation: Rotate an array right by k positions. The easy version allocates a second array; the constraint is O(1) extra space.
scenarios.prompt: How does the triple-reverse trick work?
evidence:
def rotate(a, k):
    k %= len(a)
    a.reverse()          # reverse all
    a[:k] = reversed(a[:k])      # reverse first k
    a[k:] = reversed(a[k:])      # reverse the rest
choices: Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k and the remaining n-k separately — three O(n) passes, O(1) space
Swap symmetric pairs k times — O(nk) but in place
Reverse only once — one reversal equals a rotation
In-place rotation is impossible — the extra array is required
scenarios.why: Reversing the whole array puts the last k elements first but backwards; reversing each of the two segments restores their internal order. Each element moves a constant number of times: O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space. (k %= n handles k > n; juggling cycles is the alternative single-pass method.)
scenarios.hint: What does reversing do to the positions of the last k elements — and what would un-reverse each block?

scenarios.title: The anagram check that sorts
scenarios.situation: A teammate checks anagrams by sorting both strings: O(n log n). The strings are lowercase English letters.
scenarios.prompt: How do you check anagrams in O(n)?
choices: Compare character frequency counts — anagrams are exactly strings with identical multisets of characters
Sorting is optimal for anagram detection — O(n log n) cannot be beaten
Compare the sets of characters — set(a) == set(b) ignores multiplicities correctly
XOR all characters — equal XOR means anagram
scenarios.why: Two strings are anagrams iff every character occurs the same number of times in both — a frequency-count comparison in O(n) time and O(alphabet) space. Sorting works but pays O(n log n). (Set comparison is wrong: 'aab' vs 'abb' have equal sets but are not anagrams. XOR checksums collide.)
scenarios.hint: What property, exactly, defines an anagram — order, or something countable?

scenarios.title: The dedup that must stay in place
scenarios.situation: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place, returning the new length. Extra-array solutions violate the O(1)-space constraint.
scenarios.prompt: How do the two pointers cooperate?
choices: A read pointer scans everything; a write pointer advances only on new values — sortedness means duplicates are adjacent, so one comparison per element suffices
Shift the whole tail left on each duplicate — O(n^2) but in place
Use a set to track seen values — O(n) space is acceptable in practice
Duplicates cannot be removed in place — the constraint is unsatisfiable
scenarios.why: Because the array is sorted, all copies of each value are adjacent — a[r] != a[r-1] detects exactly the first occurrence of each distinct value. The write pointer compacts those first occurrences to the front. Each element is read once and written at most once: O(n) time, O(1) space.
scenarios.hint: In a sorted array, where do duplicates sit relative to each other — and what does that let a single scan detect?

scenarios.title: The list reversed with three pointers
scenarios.situation: Reverse a singly linked list in place. Recursive solutions risk stack overflow on long lists; the iterative version is required.
scenarios.prompt: How do the three pointers rewire the list in one pass?
evidence:
def reverse(head):
    prev = None
    cur = head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next   # save before overwriting
        cur.next = prev  # flip the link
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev
choices: Save next, point cur at prev, then advance both — each link is flipped exactly once, O(n) time and O(1) space
Swap the values of symmetric nodes instead of rewiring — simpler and equivalent
Collect nodes in a stack then relink — O(n) space is fine
Recursion is the only correct way — iteration cannot reverse links
scenarios.why: The invariant: prev heads the already-reversed prefix, cur heads the unreversed suffix. Saving nxt before overwriting cur.next is the crucial step — without it the rest of the list is lost. Each iteration flips one link; after n iterations prev is the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space, no recursion depth risk.
scenarios.hint: What must you save before you overwrite cur.next — and why?

scenarios.title: The loop nobody can see
scenarios.situation: A linked list may contain a cycle. A visited-set detects it in O(n) space; the constraint is O(1) space.
scenarios.prompt: How does Floyd's tortoise-and-hare detect a cycle?
evidence:
def has_cycle(head):
    slow, fast = head, head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast: return True
    return False
choices: Two pointers move at 1x and 2x speed — in a cycle the fast one laps the slow one and they meet; without a cycle the fast one hits the end
The fast pointer jumps to the end and walks back — meeting means a cycle
Count the steps of each pointer — different counts prove a cycle
Floyd's algorithm needs a doubly linked list — it fails on singly linked
scenarios.why: On a cycle, the distance between the pointers shrinks by 1 each step (fast gains one node per round), so they must meet within one lap. Without a cycle, fast reaches the null terminator. O(n) time (at most ~2n steps), O(1) space — the classic space-for-time trade against the visited set. (The meeting point also locates the cycle start with a second phase.)
scenarios.hint: On a circular track, what happens when one runner is twice as fast as the other?

scenarios.title: The merge of two sorted lists
scenarios.situation: Merge two sorted linked lists into one sorted list. Allocating new nodes wastes the existing ones.
scenarios.prompt: How do you merge by rewiring, in O(n+m)?
evidence:
def merge(a, b):
    dummy = tail = Node(0)
    while a and b:
        if a.val <= b.val: tail.next, a = a, a.next
        else: tail.next, b = b, b.next
        tail = tail.next
    tail.next = a or b
    return dummy.next
choices: Repeatedly attach the smaller head to the tail and advance — the dummy node eliminates the empty-result special case; append the remainder when one list empties
Concatenate then sort — O((n+m) log(n+m)) is acceptable
Copy all values into an array, sort, rebuild — simpler pointer logic
Interleave nodes alternately — sortedness is preserved by alternation
scenarios.why: Both lists are sorted, so the merged head is always the smaller of the two current heads — attach it and advance that list. The dummy/sentinel node means tail always exists, removing the 'first node' special case. When one list empties, the other is already sorted and attaches whole. Each node is visited once: O(n+m), O(1) extra space.
scenarios.hint: Given two sorted lists, where must the next merged element come from?

scenarios.title: The queue built from stacks
scenarios.situation: An interviewer asks to implement a FIFO queue using only stacks, with amortized O(1) operations.
scenarios.prompt: How do two stacks make a queue?
choices: Push onto inbox; pop from outbox, refilling it by pouring inbox over (reversing order) only when empty — each element moves between stacks at most twice
Push onto both stacks and pop from either — redundancy gives FIFO
Alternate pushes between the stacks — round-robin ordering
One stack suffices — pop from the bottom with indexing
scenarios.why: Pouring inbox into outbox reverses the LIFO order into FIFO — the oldest pushed element ends up on top of outbox. Refilling only when outbox is empty means each element is moved at most twice across its lifetime: amortized O(1) per operation. The lazy transfer is the whole trick; eager transfer on every pop would be O(n).
scenarios.hint: What does moving every element from one stack to another do to their order?

scenarios.title: The middle without counting
scenarios.situation: Find the middle node of a singly linked list in one pass, without knowing the length first.
scenarios.prompt: How do the two pointers find the middle?
choices: Fast moves twice as fast — when it reaches the end, slow has covered half the distance: the middle
Slow moves backward from fast — they meet in the middle
Advance slow every other step of fast — equivalent but clearer
One pass is impossible — count first, then walk to n/2
scenarios.why: When fast has taken 2k steps, slow has taken k — slow is always halfway along fast's path. When fast can no longer advance, slow sits at the middle (the second middle for even lengths, a common convention). One pass, O(n) time, O(1) space — the same tortoise-and-hare idea as cycle detection, repurposed.
scenarios.hint: If one pointer is always twice as far along, where is the slower one when the faster finishes?

scenarios.title: The cache that forgets the right things
scenarios.situation: Design an LRU cache: get and put in O(1), evicting the least-recently-used key when full.
scenarios.prompt: Which two structures combine to give O(1) LRU?
evidence:
class LRU:
    # hash map: key -> node in doubly linked list
    # list order: most-recent at head, least-recent at tail
    # get: move node to head (splice O(1)); put: insert at head, evict tail
choices: A hash map (key to list node) plus a doubly linked list (recency order) — the map finds nodes in O(1), the list reorders/evicts in O(1)
A hash map plus a heap keyed by timestamp — O(log n) eviction is fine
A single sorted dict by access time — re-sorting on each access
A queue of keys plus linear scan — O(n) eviction is acceptable
scenarios.why: The hash map gives O(1) lookup of the node; the doubly linked list gives O(1) splice-to-front on access and O(1) tail eviction — but only doubly linked, since removing a node needs its predecessor. Either structure alone fails: the map cannot order by recency, the list cannot find by key. (Python's OrderedDict / functools.lru_cache package this pattern.)
scenarios.hint: What does each operation need — finding by key, and reordering by recency — and which structure provides each in O(1)?

scenarios.title: The BST that is not
scenarios.situation: A tree satisfies 'left < node < right' at every parent, yet a deep descendant violates the BST property. The local check passed.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the local check insufficient, and what is the correct validation?
choices: The BST property is global — each node must respect bounds inherited from all ancestors; thread (lo, hi) bounds down the recursion
Local checks are sufficient — the tree must have duplicate values
BST validation requires sorting the values first — O(n log n)
Only the root needs checking — subtrees of a valid root are valid
scenarios.why: Checking only parent-vs-child misses violations like a right-descendant of the left subtree exceeding the root. The correct invariant: every node in the left subtree is < node < every node in the right subtree — enforced by passing down (lo, hi) bounds that tighten at each level. (Equivalently, an in-order traversal of a valid BST yields sorted order.)
scenarios.hint: Which ancestors constrain a deep node's value — just its parent, or all of them?

scenarios.title: The shortest path in an unweighted graph
scenarios.situation: Find the fewest-hops route between two users in a social graph. DFS finds a route, but not the shortest one.
scenarios.prompt: Why does BFS guarantee the shortest path in unweighted graphs?
choices: BFS explores in increasing distance order — the first time the goal is dequeued, its distance is minimal, because all shorter paths were examined first
BFS is faster than DFS — speed is what guarantees optimality
The queue sorts nodes by distance — priority ordering finds the shortest
DFS with backtracking also guarantees shortest — the implementation has a bug
scenarios.why: BFS visits nodes level by level: all distance-1 nodes before distance-2, and so on. The goal's first visit therefore happens at its minimum distance — no shorter path can exist undiscovered. DFS dives deep first and may find a long path before a short one. (For weighted graphs, Dijkstra's priority queue generalizes this idea; BFS is Dijkstra with uniform weights.)
scenarios.hint: In what order does BFS first encounter nodes — and what does 'first encounter' mean for the goal?

scenarios.title: The tree that degraded to a list
scenarios.situation: A BST built from sorted input has height n, turning O(log n) operations into O(n).
scenarios.prompt: What distinguishes a balanced tree, and how do self-balancing trees maintain it?
evidence:
sorted insert 1..n into plain BST: height = n (a chain)
same input into AVL/red-black: height <= ~1.44 log2(n)
choices: Balance means height O(log n) — self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) restore it with rotations after each update, keeping the height logarithmic
Sorted input always balances trees — the implementation is buggy
Balance means equal node counts left and right — rebalance by rebuilding
Height does not affect BST operations — the slowdown is elsewhere
scenarios.why: BST operations cost O(height). Inserting sorted keys into a naive BST builds a chain — height n, operations O(n). Self-balancing trees enforce a height invariant (AVL: child heights differ by ≤1; red-black: a looser coloring rule) via rotations on insert/delete, guaranteeing O(log n) height and thus O(log n) operations with small constants.
scenarios.hint: What is the height of the degenerate tree — and what must any fix guarantee about height?

scenarios.title: The top-k without sorting everything
scenarios.situation: Find the k largest of n stream elements. Full sort is O(n log n); k is tiny compared to n.
scenarios.prompt: How does a min-heap of size k solve this in O(n log k)?
evidence:
import heapq
def top_k(stream, k):
    h = []
    for x in stream:
        heapq.heappush(h, x)
        if len(h) > k: heapq.heappop(h)  # discard smallest
    return h  # the k largest
choices: Keep a min-heap of the k largest seen so far — each new element either displaces the smallest (O(log k)) or is discarded; the heap always holds the current top-k
A max-heap of all n elements popped k times — O(n + k log n), simpler
Heaps cannot do top-k — use quickselect for O(n) average
Keep a sorted list of size k with bisect — O(nk) but simple
scenarios.why: The min-heap's root is the smallest of the current top-k — the threshold any newcomer must beat. Each element costs O(log k) heap work, total O(n log k), with O(k) memory — and it works on streams where n is unknown. (Quickselect is O(n) average but needs the full array and mutates it; the heap streams.)
scenarios.hint: If you always knew the k largest so far, what single value would tell you whether a newcomer belongs?

scenarios.title: The GPS that needs non-negative roads
scenarios.situation: Dijkstra's algorithm computes shortest paths fast, but a teammate adds 'discount' edges with negative weights and the results go wrong.
scenarios.prompt: Why does Dijkstra require non-negative weights?
evidence:
Dijkstra settles nodes in order of final distance (greedy).
Negative edge later can offer a SHORTER path to an already-settled node -> wrong answer.
Fix: Bellman-Ford handles negatives (slower); or reweight (Johnson).
choices: Dijkstra's greedy settling assumes the first time a node is extracted its distance is final — a negative edge can later undercut it, breaking the invariant
Negative weights cause infinite loops — the algorithm never terminates
Priority queues cannot hold negative keys — use a FIFO queue instead
Dijkstra works with negatives if you initialize distances to negative infinity
scenarios.why: Dijkstra extracts the unsettled node with smallest tentative distance and declares it final — valid only because non-negative edges cannot provide a shorter route to it later. A negative edge can: a settled node's distance may still improve, silently producing wrong answers. Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges n-1 times (O(VE)) and additionally detects negative cycles.
scenarios.hint: What promise does Dijkstra make the moment it removes a node from the priority queue — and which edge type can break that promise afterward?

scenarios.title: The build order with a cycle
scenarios.situation: Tasks have dependencies; compute a valid execution order. One dependency set contains a cycle, and naive DFS ordering silently produces an invalid schedule.
scenarios.prompt: How does topological sort work, and how does it expose cycles?
choices: Kahn's algorithm peels off zero-in-degree nodes iteratively — if nodes remain unpeeled, a cycle exists and no valid order is possible
DFS finishing order always yields a valid schedule, cycles included
Cycles are impossible in dependency graphs — validate the input instead
Sort tasks alphabetically — dependencies resolve by name order
scenarios.why: A topological order exists iff the graph is a DAG. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with no remaining prerequisites; each removal can only enable valid next steps. If the process stalls with nodes left, those nodes depend on each other circularly — a cycle, which is both the diagnosis and the proof that no schedule exists. (DFS-based topo sort detects cycles via back edges / node coloring.)
scenarios.hint: Which tasks are safe to run first — and what does it mean if no task ever becomes safe?

scenarios.title: The partition that does the real work
scenarios.situation: A teammate implements quicksort's recursion but hand-waves the partition step, producing an O(n^2) 'sort' that barely sorts.
scenarios.prompt: What is partition's contract, and why does Lomuto/Hoare matter?
choices: Partition rearranges so the pivot lands in its final sorted position with smaller elements left and larger right — recursion then sorts each side independently
Partition fully sorts the segment — the recursion is just verification
The pivot must be the median — Lomuto with last-element pivot is incorrect
Partition is O(n log n) by itself — quicksort's total is O(n log^2 n)
scenarios.why: Partition's postcondition — pivot at index i, everything left ≤ pivot ≤ everything right — is what makes the recursion valid: the pivot never moves again, and the two sides are independent subproblems. Lomuto is simple but does extra swaps with duplicates; Hoare's scheme (two inward pointers) does fewer swaps and is the common library choice. Either way, the contract — not the scheme — is the point.
scenarios.hint: After partition returns i, what do you know about a[i] versus every other element — and why does that let the recursion split?

scenarios.title: The sort that preserves order
scenarios.situation: Records sorted by name must keep their original relative order for equal names (a prior timestamp sort). Quicksort scrambles the ties.
scenarios.prompt: Why is merge sort stable, and what does stability cost?
evidence:
input:  [(amy,2), (bob,1), (amy,1)] sorted by name
stable result:  [(amy,2), (amy,1), (bob,1)]  -- original order kept for ties
quicksort may give: [(amy,1), (amy,2), (bob,1)]
choices: Merge sort is stable because merging takes from the left half on ties — the cost is O(n) auxiliary space (or careful in-place merging)
Stability is automatic for all O(n log n) sorts — quicksort's result was a bug
Stability requires extra key columns — add the timestamp to the sort key
Merge sort is unstable like quicksort — use insertion sort for stability
scenarios.why: A sort is stable if equal keys retain their input order. Merge sort's merge step breaks ties toward the left half, which holds earlier elements — stability falls out naturally. The price is the O(n) merge buffer (standard implementations allocate it once). When stability matters (multi-key sorts, UI lists), it is a requirement, not a nicety.
scenarios.hint: When the merge step sees equal keys from both halves, which side should win to preserve input order?

scenarios.title: The binary search that misses the edges
scenarios.situation: A hand-written binary search works for middle elements but fails on the first and last, and once looped forever.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct loop invariant and bound update?
evidence:
def bsearch(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a) - 1
    while lo <= hi:              # invariant: answer in [lo, hi] if present
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == x: return mid
        elif a[mid] < x: lo = mid + 1   # exclude mid: it is too small
        else: hi = mid - 1              # exclude mid: it is too big
    return -1
choices: Maintain 'answer in [lo,hi] if present': loop while lo <= hi, and exclude mid itself (mid±1) since it was just tested — this terminates with no missed edges
Use lo < hi and set lo = mid — fewer updates, same result
mid = (lo+hi)//2 overflows — use (lo+hi)//2 only for small arrays
Binary search cannot find edge elements — check them separately first
scenarios.why: The two classic bugs: (1) lo = mid instead of mid+1 can stall (when lo+1 == hi, mid == lo, no progress — infinite loop); excluding the tested mid guarantees progress. (2) lo < hi with inclusive-hi indexing skips checking the final single element. The invariant 'the answer, if present, lies within [lo, hi]' plus shrinking the interval every step gives correctness and termination. (In fixed-width languages, lo + (hi-lo)//2 avoids overflow.)
scenarios.hint: After testing a[mid], is mid still a candidate — and what happens to progress if you keep it?

scenarios.title: The linear sort for bounded keys
scenarios.situation: Sort a million exam scores (0-100). Comparison sorts take O(n log n); the keys' tiny range suggests better.
scenarios.prompt: How does counting sort beat the comparison-sort lower bound?
choices: Count occurrences of each key value, then emit values in order — O(n+k) time, valid because keys are bounded integers, not arbitrary comparable objects
The Ω(n log n) lower bound applies to all sorts — counting sort must be wrong
Counting sort is O(n) only for distinct keys — duplicates break it
It beats the bound by using extra memory — space always trades for time
scenarios.why: The n log n lower bound applies only to comparison-based sorts. Counting sort never compares elements — it indexes by key value, which requires keys to be small integers (range k). Time O(n+k), space O(k): brilliant when k is small, useless when keys are arbitrary (strings, floats) or k >> n.
scenarios.hint: What assumption about the keys lets you index instead of compare — and what does the lower bound assume?

scenarios.title: The binary search on rotated data
scenarios.situation: A sorted array was rotated at an unknown pivot: [4,5,6,1,2,3]. Plain binary search fails.
scenarios.prompt: How do you restore O(log n) search?
evidence:
def search_rot(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)-1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo+hi)//2
        if a[mid] == x: return mid
        if a[lo] <= a[mid]:  # left half sorted
            if a[lo] <= x < a[mid]: hi = mid-1
            else: lo = mid+1
        else:  # right half sorted
            if a[mid] < x <= a[hi]: lo = mid+1
            else: hi = mid-1
    return -1
choices: One half is always sorted — identify it via a[lo] <= a[mid], then decide whether x lies in that sorted half or the other one
Un-rotate the array first (O(n)), then binary search — O(n) total is fine
Rotated arrays cannot be searched sublinearly — fall back to linear scan
Find the pivot with linear scan, then binary search each half
scenarios.why: Rotation preserves a key property: at every step, at least one half of [lo,hi] is sorted. Comparing a[lo] ≤ a[mid] identifies which. If x falls inside the sorted half's range, search there; otherwise search the unsorted half (which still halves). Each step discards half: O(log n). (With duplicates, the worst case degrades — a[lo]==a[mid] is ambiguous.)
scenarios.hint: After rotation, what is still true about at least one of the two halves around mid?

scenarios.title: The kth smallest without sorting
scenarios.situation: Find the median (kth smallest) of n unsorted numbers. Full sort is O(n log n); only one order statistic is needed.
scenarios.prompt: How does quickselect achieve O(n) average?
evidence:
def quickselect(a, k):
    # partition around a pivot like quicksort,
    # then recurse ONLY into the side containing index k
    # average: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = 2n = O(n)
choices: Partition like quicksort but recurse into only the side containing k — the work halves geometrically: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(n) average
Quickselect is O(n log n) like quicksort — the name is misleading
Heap of size k gives O(n) — quickselect is never the right tool
The median requires sorting by definition — accept O(n log n)
scenarios.why: After partitioning, the pivot's final index p is known: if p == k done; if p > k the answer is left; else right (adjusting k). Only one side is explored, so average work is n + n/2 + n/4 + ... < 2n. Worst case is O(n^2) with bad pivots (median-of-medians gives deterministic O(n) but with heavy constants — rarely used in practice).
scenarios.hint: After one partition, how many of the two sides can possibly contain the kth element?

scenarios.title: The exponential Fibonacci
scenarios.situation: Naive recursive Fibonacci takes minutes for n=50. The recursion tree recomputes the same subproblems endlessly.
scenarios.prompt: How does memoization change the complexity?
choices: Cache each subproblem's result — the recursion DAG has n distinct states, so total work drops from O(2^n) to O(n)
Memoization only helps for n > 100 — the overhead dominates below that
lru_cache makes it O(1) — every call after the first is a cache hit
The exponential is inherent — memoization just hides it with threads
scenarios.why: Naive fib recomputes fib(k) exponentially many times — the recursion tree has O(2^n) nodes but only n distinct subproblems. Memoization computes each distinct state once: n states × O(1) work each = O(n) time, O(n) space for the cache (plus O(n) stack depth). The pattern: overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure = DP candidate.
scenarios.hint: How many distinct values of fib(k) exist for k ≤ n — and how many times does the naive version compute each?

scenarios.title: The table you barely need
scenarios.situation: A bottom-up Fibonacci keeps the whole dp array, using O(n) space. Only the last two values are ever read.
scenarios.prompt: How do you reduce the space, and when is it safe?
evidence:
def fib(n):
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n): a, b = b, a + b
    return a  # O(n) time, O(1) space
choices: Keep only the states the recurrence actually reads — fib(n) needs fib(n-1) and fib(n-2), so two variables suffice: O(1) space
Space reduction changes the answer — the full table is required for correctness
Use a deque of size n//2 — halves the space while staying safe
Tabulation always needs the full table — switch to memoization for less space
scenarios.why: Space optimization is safe when the recurrence has bounded lookback: if dp[i] depends only on dp[i-1..i-k], keep a sliding window of k values. Fibonacci's lookback is 2, so two variables replace the array. The rule generalizes: identify the dependency footprint first, then size the storage to it — but keep the full table when you must reconstruct the actual solution path, not just its value.
scenarios.hint: Which earlier entries does dp[i] actually read — all of them, or just the recent ones?

scenarios.title: The thief with a weight limit
scenarios.situation: Choose items (each with weight and value) to maximize value without exceeding capacity W. Greedy by value-density fails.
scenarios.prompt: What is the 0/1 knapsack recurrence?
evidence:
dp[i][w] = max value using first i items with capacity w
dp[i][w] = dp[i-1][w]                                  # skip item i
if wt[i] <= w:
    dp[i][w] = max(dp[i][w], dp[i-1][w-wt[i]] + val[i])  # take item i
choices: dp[i][w] = max(skip i, take i + best of remaining capacity) — each item is used at most once, hence dp[i-1] in both branches
Sort by value/weight ratio and take greedily — optimal for 0/1 knapsack
dp[w] = max value for exact weight w, trying items in any order with unlimited reuse
Knapsack is NP-hard so no recurrence exists — use brute force
scenarios.why: The 0/1 choice is per item: either skip item i (best of first i-1 with capacity w) or take it (its value plus best of first i-1 with capacity w-wt[i]). Referencing dp[i-1] (not dp[i]) enforces single use — dp[i][...] on the take branch would allow reuse, which is the unbounded variant. Complexity O(nW): pseudopolynomial — polynomial in n and W, exponential in the input's bit length.
scenarios.hint: For item i, what are the two options — and which subproblem does each option reduce to?

scenarios.title: The diff that finds common ground
scenarios.situation: A diff tool needs the longest common subsequence of two strings — the backbone that a minimal edit script is built around.
scenarios.prompt: What is the LCS recurrence?
choices: If the characters match, take 1 plus the LCS of the remainders; otherwise take the better of skipping a character from either string
Count matching characters position by position — LCS is just positional matches
LCS equals the longest common substring — use a sliding window
Compare lengths first — the shorter string bounds the LCS trivially
scenarios.why: Optimal substructure: if a[i]==b[j], some optimal LCS uses both (any optimal solution can be rearranged to include them); if they differ, at least one of them is unused in every optimal solution, so drop it from either side and take the max. Fill the table bottom-up (or memoize top-down): O(nm) time and space, O(min(n,m)) space with rolling rows.
scenarios.hint: If the first characters match, must an optimal solution use them? If they differ, can both be used?

scenarios.title: The greedy change that is not optimal
scenarios.situation: A vending machine uses greedy change (largest coin first). With coin denominations [1, 3, 4] and amount 6, it returns 4+1+1 (3 coins) instead of 3+3 (2 coins).
scenarios.prompt: Why does greedy fail here, and what is the DP formulation?
evidence:
dp[x] = min coins for amount x
dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x - c] for c in coins if c <= x)
# dp[6] = 1 + dp[3] = 2  (greedy gave 3)
choices: Greedy is optimal only for canonical coin systems — in general, dp[x] = 1 + min over coins of dp[x-c]; greedy's local choice can block the global optimum
Greedy always gives optimal change — the machine's coin set must contain a counterfeit
DP is overkill — sort coins ascending instead of descending
The DP is O(amount × coins) which is worse than greedy's O(coins)
scenarios.why: Greedy commits to the largest coin without considering how the remainder decomposes — 4 leaves 2 = 1+1, while skipping 4 allows 3+3. The DP considers every first-coin choice: dp[x] tries each coin c and takes 1 + dp[x-c]. Greedy works for canonical systems (US coins) but that is a property needing proof per system, not a general truth.
scenarios.hint: Does taking the biggest coin first always leave the easiest remainder — or can it paint you into a corner?

scenarios.title: The increasing subsequence in O(n log n)
scenarios.situation: Find the length of the longest increasing subsequence. The O(n^2) DP (dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] for j<i, a[j]<a[i]) is too slow for n=10^5.
scenarios.prompt: How does patience sorting achieve O(n log n)?
evidence:
import bisect
piles = []
for x in a:
    i = bisect.bisect_left(piles, x)
    if i == len(piles): piles.append(x)
    else: piles[i] = x
# len(piles) == length of LIS
choices: Maintain piles where each pile top is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of that length — binary search places each element in O(log n)
Sort the array first — the LIS of a sorted array is the array itself
Patience sorting only works for strictly decreasing sequences
O(n log n) is impossible — LIS has an Ω(n^2) lower bound
scenarios.why: Process elements left to right, maintaining piles[i] = smallest tail value of any increasing subsequence of length i+1 seen so far. Each x either extends the longest pile (append) or improves an earlier pile's tail (replace via binary search) — the piles stay sorted, so placement is O(log n). len(piles) equals the LIS length. (Recovering the actual subsequence needs parent pointers — the length trick alone does not reconstruct it.)
scenarios.hint: For each possible subsequence length, what single number summarizes 'the best subsequence of that length so far'?

lessons.title: Complexity Analysis — Core concepts
concepts: Big-O describes growth rate as n→∞: the fastest-growing term eventually dwarfs the rest, so O(n^2 + n log n + n) simplifies to O(n^2).
Sequential phases add (not multiply) — multiplication applies to nested loops.

Amortized analysis averages the total cost of a sequence; it does not promise any single operation is cheap (a latency-sensitive system may still prefer pre-sized arrays). Space analysis must count the call stack, not just allocated containers.
Geometric series: resizes at sizes 1,2,4,...,n copy 1+2+4+...+n = 2n-1 total elements — a geometric series bounded by 2n.

example.walkthrough: Each recursive call holds a stack frame until its children return, so peak stack depth equals the longest root-to-leaf path: the tree height h. Balanced trees give O(log n); a degenerate chain gives O(n) — enough to overflow the call stack.

pitfalls: Common trap: recursion uses no extra space beyond the input.
Common trap: binary search examines log n elements per step.
Common trap: the worst single append dominates the analysis.
Common trap: every node gets a stack frame simultaneously.

lessons.title: Arrays & Strings — Core concepts
concepts: Two strings are anagrams iff every character occurs the same number of times in both — a frequency-count comparison in O(n) time and O(alphabet) space. Reversing the whole array puts the last k elements first but backwards; reversing each of the two segments restores their internal order.

Sorted array techniques: because the array is sorted, all copies of each value are adjacent — a[r] != a[r-1] detects exactly the first occurrence of each distinct value. (Segment trees/Fenwick trees answer in O(log n) but support point updates — the right tool when the array changes; prefix sums win for static data.).
Sliding window: the window [lo, hi] always holds a valid (duplicate-free) substring. hi advances n times total; lo only moves forward (at most n times).
Prefix sums: p[r+1] - P[l] cancels the shared prefix: (a0+...+ar) - (a0+...+a{l-1}) = a{l}+...+ar.
Preprocessing is O(n) time and space; every query is O(1).

example.walkthrough: Two strings are anagrams iff every character occurs the same number of times in both — a frequency-count comparison in O(n) time and O(alphabet) space. Sorting works but pays O(n log n). (Set comparison is wrong: 'aab' vs 'abb' have equal sets but are not anagrams.

pitfalls: Common trap: two pointers only work on unsorted arrays.
Common trap: range sums are faster on sorted data.
Common trap: one reversal equals a rotation.
Common trap: use two nested loops but break early on duplicates.

lessons.title: Linked Structures — Core concepts
concepts: Two pointers: both lists are sorted, so the merged head is always the smaller of the two current heads — attach it and advance that list. On a cycle, the distance between the pointers shrinks by 1 each step (fast gains one node per round), so they must meet within one lap.

Linked list reversal: the hash map gives O(1) lookup of the node; the doubly linked list gives O(1) splice-to-front on access and O(1) tail eviction — but only doubly linked, since removing a node needs its predecessor.
Cycle detection: one pass, O(n) time, O(1) space — the same tortoise-and-hare idea as cycle detection, repurposed. Without a cycle, fast reaches the null terminator.

example.code:
class LRU:
    # hash map: key -> node in doubly linked list
    # list order: most-recent at head, least-recent at tail
    # get: move node to head (splice O(1)); put: insert at head, evict tail
example.walkthrough: The hash map gives O(1) lookup of the node; the doubly linked list gives O(1) splice-to-front on access and O(1) tail eviction — but only doubly linked, since removing a node needs its predecessor. Either structure alone fails: the map cannot order by recency, the list cannot find by key. (Python's OrderedDict / functools.lru_cache package this pattern.).

pitfalls: Common trap: floyd's algorithm needs a doubly linked list.
Common trap: a hash map plus a heap keyed by timestamp.
Common trap: a single sorted dict by access time.
Common trap: swap the values of symmetric nodes instead of rewiring.

lessons.title: Trees & Graphs — Core concepts
concepts: BST validation: (Equivalently, an in-order traversal of a valid BST yields sorted order.). BST operations cost O(height).
Bounds threading: the correct invariant: every node in the left subtree is < node < every node in the right subtree — enforced by passing down (lo, hi) bounds that tighten at each level.
BFS: (For weighted graphs, Dijkstra's priority queue generalizes this idea; BFS is Dijkstra with uniform weights.).
Shortest path: the goal's first visit therefore happens at its minimum distance — no shorter path can exist undiscovered.

example.walkthrough: A topological order exists iff the graph is a DAG. Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes with no remaining prerequisites; each removal can only enable valid next steps. If the process stalls with nodes left, those nodes depend on each other circularly — a cycle, which is both the diagnosis and the proof that no schedule exists.

pitfalls: Common trap: BST validation requires sorting the values first.
Common trap: dijkstra works with negatives if you initialize distances to negative infinity.
Common trap: negative weights cause infinite loops.
Common trap: DFS with backtracking also guarantees shortest.

Overlapping subproblems: the pattern: overlapping subproblems + optimal substructure = DP candidate.

lessons.title: Data Structures & Algorithms — Core concepts
concepts: Big-O describes growth: O(1) constant, O(log n) halving, O(n) linear, O(n log n) efficient sorting, O(n^2) nested loops, O(2^n) brute force. Analyze the dominant term for large n, but remember constants and the actual n decide real-world winners.

Choose structures by access pattern: hash tables for O(1) membership without ordering, balanced trees for ordered data and range queries, heaps for repeated min/max extraction, tries for prefix queries. The wrong structure turns a linear algorithm quadratic.

Trees and graphs are traversed, not just stored: BFS (queue, level order) gives shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS (stack/recursion, depth-first) suits topological sort, cycle detection, and exhaustive search. Recursion depth is a real budget — Python's default limit is 1000 frames.

Sorting is O(n log n) in the general comparison case (mergesort, heapsort, introsort); quicksort is fast on average but needs a randomized pivot or depth cutoff to avoid O(n^2) adversarial input. Stability (equal elements keep order) matters when sorting by multiple keys in passes.

Dynamic programming solves overlapping subproblems once: identify the recurrence and the state, then implement top-down with memoization or bottom-up tabulation. Memoization keeps the natural recursion but inherits stack depth; tabulation is iterative and lets you compress state to O(1)–O(k) space.

Greedy algorithms commit locally and never backtrack — they demand proof. The exchange argument (swap an optimal solution's first choice for the greedy one without harming it) is the standard tool; when it fails, reach for DP instead of hoping.

example.walkthrough: The deque is the BFS frontier: popleft expands nodes in order of distance from start, so the first time we pop the goal its path is shortest. The seen set prevents re-exploration — without it, cyclic graphs loop forever.

pitfalls: Common trap: `x in list` inside a loop — O(n) per check makes the loop quadratic; use a set.
Common trap: assuming recursion is free — deep recursion overflows the stack; prefer iteration or raise limits deliberately.
Common trap: using DFS when you need shortest path — only BFS (unweighted) or Dijkstra (weighted) certify minimality.
Common trap: sorting with a bad pivot strategy on untrusted input — adversarial data turns quicksort quadratic.

simulations.title: Cycle or dead end?
simulations.brief: A traversal of a linked structure visits A → B → C → B → C → B … Decide what you are looking at.

steps.text: The visit sequence repeats B → C → B → C. First conclusion?

choices.label: There is a cycle: some node's next points back to an earlier node
choices.feedback: Right — a repeated subsequence in the visit order is the fingerprint of a cycle.

choices.label: The list is just long
choices.feedback: A long list never revisits nodes. Repetition means a cycle.

choices.label: The traversal code has an off-by-one
choices.feedback: Off-by-one skips or duplicates one node; it never loops forever.

steps.text: How do you confirm the cycle without using memory proportional to n?

choices.label: Floyd's tortoise and hare: two pointers at different speeds; they meet inside the cycle
choices.feedback: Floyd's uses O(1) space: the meeting proves the cycle, then a second pass finds its start.

choices.label: Store every visited node in a set
choices.feedback: Works, but costs O(n) space — the question asked for constant space.

choices.label: Reverse the list and see what happens
choices.feedback: Reversing a cyclic list never terminates.

steps.text: Tortoise and hare meet at C. What do you do next?

choices.label: Reset one pointer to the head and advance both at equal speed; they meet at the cycle start
choices.feedback: Classic result: the second meeting point is the cycle's entry node.

choices.label: Delete node C
choices.feedback: Deleting the meeting node doesn't identify the entry — and it mutates the structure.

simulations.debrief: Repeated visits mean a cycle. Floyd's algorithm detects it in O(1) space, and the two-phase pointer walk finds the entry node.
